title: Plain Omelette
subtitle: Three eggs, butter, and thirty seconds, the classic French technique
excerpt: A plain French omelette is pale gold outside, just-set inside, and rolled in the pan in under a minute. Speed and a hot pan are what make it work.
sourceNotes: The French plain omelette technique, hot pan, foaming butter, rapid movement, is the standard taught in classical French cookery and documented by Escoffier and Julia Child. The method has been the benchmark for egg cookery since the nineteenth century.

glossaryTerms.definition: In omelette-making, rolling the cooked egg over on itself in the pan to enclose the centre and form a neat, closed shape, done with a spatula or by tilting the pan and using the lip to help roll the omelette onto the plate.

content.text: A French plain omelette is the most demanding thirty seconds in basic cookery. The pan must be properly hot, the butter must foam and begin to subside before the eggs go in, and from that moment everything moves fast. The finished omelette is pale gold on the outside, barely set on the inside, and

into a neat cylinder before it leaves the pan. It takes practice, the first few will likely be browned or overcooked, but once the technique is in your hands it takes less than two minutes from cold eggs to plate.

Crack the {{eggs}} eggs into a bowl and beat them briskly with a fork or balloon whisk for about thirty seconds, long enough to fully combine the yolks and whites into an even, pale yellow mixture. Season with a pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes and {{black-pepper}} black pepper. Do not add milk or cream: a classic French omelette uses nothing but egg. Milk loosens the mixture and slows the set; cream makes it richer but changes the texture.

A 20 cm non-stick frying pan is the right size for a three-egg omelette. Put it over a medium-high heat for a full minute before anything goes in, the pan needs to be properly hot, not just warm. Add the {{unsalted-butter}} butter and watch it melt. It will foam immediately, and then, after ten to fifteen seconds, the foam will begin to subside. That is the moment. Swirl the pan to coat it, then pour in the egg mixture all at once.

The moment the egg goes in, grip the pan handle firmly and shake the pan rapidly back and forth over the heat while simultaneously drawing a silicone spatula across the base in short strokes. The shaking keeps the egg moving and the spatula breaks up the setting curds. This continues for twenty to thirty seconds. The eggs will look almost done, still slightly wet on top, when you stop moving them. Tip the pan away from you at about a 45-degree angle so the egg slides to the far edge.

With the pan tilted, use the spatula to fold the near third of the omelette over the centre. Then tip the pan further and roll the omelette onto the plate, letting the far edge fold underneath as it lands. The finished shape is a closed cylinder, pale gold outside. If it is brown in patches, the pan was too hot or the cooking took too long, pace yourself through the practice rather than rushing to correct it. Speed is the goal, but controlled speed, not panic.

A properly made plain omelette is pale, not white, not browned. The outside has just a trace of colour from the butter. Press the top with a finger and it should feel just set, with a little give. Cut it open and the centre should be baveuse, softly set and slightly glossy, not raw, not dry. Getting this right every time is what separates a cook who has made a hundred omelettes from one who has made three.

Omelette is brown and rubbery: the pan was too hot or the cooking went on too long. The whole process from egg going in to rolling should take no more than forty-five seconds. If it is taking longer, your heat is too low and you are overcooking while waiting for it to set.

Omelette is sticking to the pan: the pan is not properly non-stick or was not hot enough when the butter went in. Make sure the pan is hot before the butter, and use a pan you know is non-stick, an omelette on a stainless or cast-iron pan requires much more skill and fat.

Omelette tears when rolling: the egg is slightly overcooked and has become firm and inflexible. Pull the pan off the heat a moment earlier, the egg should still have a thin layer of wet mixture on top when you begin to roll it.
